events.s: Abrahah, ruler of Yemen, marched on Makkah with an army and elephants to destroy the Ka‘bah. Allah protected His House, sending flocks of birds that pelted the army with stones of baked clay. Surah al-Fil recalls the event. The Prophet ﷺ was born in this same year.
events.l: Allah protects what is His; no army is greater than His command.

events.s: Muhammad ibn ‘Abdullah was born into the clan of Hashim of the tribe of Quraysh. His father had died before his birth. He was sent as an infant to the desert with his wet-nurse Halimah of Banu Sa‘d, where he grew up strong and pure-spoken.
events.l: Allah raises His chosen ones from humble, difficult beginnings.

events.t: Loss of his mother and grandfather
events.s: His mother Aminah died when he was about six, on the way back from Yathrib. His grandfather ‘Abd al-Muttalib cared for him until he too died two years later, after which his uncle Abu Talib raised him with great love.
events.l: Orphanhood did not diminish him — Allah Himself sheltered him (Quran 93:6).

events.s: Known as al-Amin, the trustworthy, he traded on behalf of Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a respected businesswoman. Impressed by his honesty and character she proposed marriage. She became his greatest support and the mother of most of his children.
events.l: Honesty in work opens doors; a righteous spouse is a great blessing.

events.s: When Quraysh rebuilt the Ka‘bah, the clans nearly came to blows over who would place the Black Stone. They agreed to let the next man to enter decide — it was Muhammad ﷺ. He placed the stone on a cloth, had every clan lift it together, and set it in place himself.
events.l: Wisdom and fairness can turn conflict into unity.

events.s: At about forty, while in retreat in the cave of Hira, the angel Jibril came to him with the first words of the Quran: “Read in the name of your Lord who created.” Shaken, he returned to Khadijah, who comforted him and became the first to believe.
events.l: Knowledge and reading are where the message begins.

events.s: After about three years of private invitation, he was commanded to warn his clan openly. Standing on Safa he called Quraysh together and invited them to worship Allah alone. Many mocked him, and opposition and persecution began to grow.
events.l: Truth must be spoken clearly, even when it is unpopular.

events.s: To escape persecution, a group of Muslims migrated to Abyssinia, ruled by a just Christian king, the Negus. When Quraysh sent envoys to bring them back, Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib recited from Surah Maryam, and the Negus wept and granted them protection.
events.l: Justice can be found among people of other faiths; truth moves sincere hearts.

events.s: Hamzah, the Prophet’s uncle, embraced Islam after defending him from Abu Jahl. Soon after, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab — once a fierce opponent — accepted Islam after reading verses of Surah Ta-Ha. Their conversion gave the Muslims new strength.
events.l: Hearts are in Allah’s hands; never give up on anyone.

events.s: Quraysh boycotted Banu Hashim, refusing to trade or marry with them. For about three years the Prophet’s clan was confined to a valley and suffered hunger. The boycott eventually collapsed when some Makkans spoke out against its injustice.
events.l: Patience through hardship; injustice does not last.

events.s: Within a short time both Abu Talib, his protector, and Khadijah, his beloved wife, passed away. With their loss the persecution became harsher, and this year became known as the Year of Sorrow.
events.l: Even the best of people feel grief; it is part of being human.

events.s: He travelled to Ta’if hoping its people would accept the message. Instead they rejected him and set children to throw stones until his feet bled. When the angel of the mountains offered to crush the town, he refused, hoping their descendants would worship Allah.
events.l: Mercy over revenge — even to those who hurt you.

events.s: In one night he was taken from Makkah to al-Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem, where he led the prophets in prayer, then ascended through the heavens. On this journey the five daily prayers were made obligatory.
events.l: Salah is a gift given directly in the heavens — the believer’s own ascent.

events.s: Men from Yathrib met him during the pilgrimage season and accepted Islam. The next year a larger group pledged to protect him as they would their own families, opening the way for the Muslims to migrate to their city.
events.l: Allah opens a door when others close.

events.s: As Quraysh plotted to kill him, he left Makkah by night with Abu Bakr, hiding three days in the cave of Thawr. They reached Quba and then Yathrib, which became Madinat an-Nabi — the City of the Prophet. The Islamic calendar begins from this year.
events.l: Trust in Allah while taking every practical means.

events.s: He built a simple mosque of mud brick and palm trunks, working alongside his companions. It became the centre of worship, learning, and community life. He also joined the emigrants and helpers as brothers, sharing homes and wealth.
events.l: Community is built on worship and real brotherhood.

events.s: A written agreement set out the rights and duties of the city’s Muslim and Jewish tribes, establishing mutual defence and justice under one community.
events.l: Islam brought law, order and protection for all citizens.

events.s: After praying towards Jerusalem for about sixteen months, the Muslims were commanded to face the Ka‘bah in Makkah. The direction of prayer has been the Ka‘bah ever since.
events.l: Obedience to Allah’s command is the heart of worship.

events.s: About 313 poorly-equipped Muslims met a Makkan army roughly three times larger. Allah granted a decisive victory, which the Quran calls the Day of Criterion. Fasting in Ramadan was made obligatory in the same year.
events.l: Victory comes from Allah, not numbers.

events.s: The Muslims were winning until archers left their post against orders. The tide turned, the Prophet ﷺ was wounded, and around seventy companions were martyred, including his uncle Hamzah.
events.l: Disobedience has consequences; setbacks are lessons, not the end.

events.s: A coalition of about ten thousand besieged Madinah. On Salman al-Farisi’s advice the Muslims dug a trench across the open northern approach. After weeks of siege, a fierce wind and divisions among the attackers broke the coalition.
events.l: Good ideas can come from anyone; Allah sends help in unexpected ways.

events.s: Travelling to perform umrah, the Muslims were stopped outside Makkah. A ten-year truce was agreed whose terms seemed unfavourable — yet the Quran called it a clear victory, and in the peace that followed Islam spread faster than ever.
events.l: What looks like a loss may be the greatest gain.

events.s: The Prophet ﷺ sent letters inviting rulers to Islam, including Heraclius of Byzantium, the Persian emperor, the Negus and the ruler of Egypt. Heraclius questioned Abu Sufyan closely about the Prophet’s character.
events.l: The message is for all of humanity.

events.s: After repeated hostility from Khaybar, the Muslims besieged and took its fortresses. The land was left with its people to farm in return for half the harvest.
events.l: Strength combined with fair terms.

events.s: After Quraysh broke the treaty, the Prophet ﷺ marched on Makkah with ten thousand. The city was taken almost without fighting. He cleared the Ka‘bah of idols and forgave his former persecutors, saying they were free to go.
events.l: Forgiveness at the moment of power is the mark of true greatness.

events.s: Soon after, the tribes of Hawazin gathered a large army. At first the Muslims were caught off guard and scattered, proud of their numbers, but they regrouped and were victorious.
events.l: Never rely on numbers or pride.

events.t: Tabuk and the Year of Delegations
events.s: The Prophet ﷺ led a large army to Tabuk in extreme heat against a Byzantine threat; no battle took place. That year, delegations from across Arabia came to Madinah to accept Islam.
events.l: Sincerity is tested in hardship; hypocrisy is exposed.

events.s: He performed his only Hajj with over a hundred thousand people. At ‘Arafah he gave the Farewell Sermon: the sanctity of life, wealth and honour; rights of women; the equality of all people; and holding fast to the Quran.
events.l: No Arab is better than a non-Arab, nor any colour above another, except by taqwa.

events.t: The passing of the Prophet ﷺ
events.s: After a short illness he passed away in the home of ‘A’ishah, aged about sixty-three. Abu Bakr steadied the grieving community: “Whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worships Allah, Allah is Ever-Living and never dies.”
events.l: Our attachment is to Allah, and to the message the Prophet ﷺ left us.

events.s: The Prophet’s closest friend became the first caliph. He held the community together through the ridda wars and began compiling the Quran into a single written collection after many memorisers were martyred.
events.l: Steadfastness in a crisis protects the whole community.

events.s: Under ‘Umar the Muslim state grew to include Iraq, Syria and Egypt, and Jerusalem was received peacefully. He founded the Hijri calendar, public registers and stipends, and was famous for his justice and accountability.
events.l: Leadership is service and answerability.

events.s: Known for his generosity and modesty, ‘Uthman sent standard copies of the Quran to the major cities, unifying its recitation in writing. His caliphate ended with his murder by rebels.
events.l: Preserving the Quran is a trust for every generation.

events.s: The Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law, known for his knowledge and courage, led the community through a period of civil strife. He was assassinated in Kufa in 40 AH.
events.l: Knowledge, justice and patience in times of division.

events.s: Ruling from Damascus, the Umayyads expanded the lands of Islam from Spain to Central Asia. They built the Dome of the Rock and the Great Mosque of Damascus, and made Arabic the language of administration.
events.l: Faith reached three continents within a century.

events.s: A short but celebrated reign. He was known for justice, simplicity and care for the poor, and is often counted by scholars as a fifth rightly-guided caliph.
events.l: One sincere leader can transform a society.

events.t: The Abbasids and the House of Wisdom
events.s: The Abbasids founded Baghdad, which became a world centre of learning. Scholars at the House of Wisdom translated and advanced mathematics, medicine, astronomy and philosophy — al-Khwarizmi’s algebra among them.
events.l: Seeking knowledge is worship when done for Allah.

events.t: The great imams and hadith scholars
events.s: Imams Abu Hanifah, Malik, ash-Shafi‘i and Ahmad laid the foundations of the four schools of law, while al-Bukhari, Muslim and others compiled the major hadith collections.
events.l: The Sunnah was preserved by people who devoted their lives to it.

events.s: Muslim rule in Iberia produced Córdoba, one of the greatest cities of its age, with libraries, scholars and architecture such as the Great Mosque of Córdoba and later the Alhambra. Granada, the last emirate, fell in 1492.
events.l: Civilisations rise with knowledge and unity, and fall with division.

events.s: After the Battle of Hattin, Salahuddin al-Ayyubi recovered Jerusalem. In contrast to the massacre of 1099, he allowed its inhabitants to leave safely, and became renowned for his chivalry.
events.l: Strength with mercy honours the faith.

events.s: The Mongols sacked Baghdad, ending the Abbasid caliphate there and destroying libraries. Two years later the Mamluks halted the Mongol advance at ‘Ayn Jalut.
events.l: Even great civilisations can fall; renewal is always possible.

events.s: Sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople, which became Istanbul, the Ottoman capital for centuries. The Ottomans went on to rule much of the Muslim world and served the Two Holy Mosques.
events.l: Perseverance and planning across generations.

events.s: After World War I the Ottoman state was dissolved and the caliphate was formally abolished in 1924, giving way to modern nation states across the Muslim world.
events.l: The ummah’s bond is faith, beyond any border.

ten: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
The Prophet’s closest friend and first adult male to believe; first caliph.
‘Umar ibn al-Khattab
Al-Faruq, who distinguished truth from falsehood; second caliph, famed for justice.
‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan
Dhun-Nurayn, married to two of the Prophet’s daughters; third caliph who unified the written Quran.
‘Ali ibn Abi Talib
The Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law; fourth caliph, renowned for knowledge and bravery.
Talhah ibn ‘Ubaydullah
Shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his own body at Uhud; known for great generosity.
az-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam
The Prophet’s cousin and ‘disciple’ (hawari); among the earliest Muslims.
‘Abd ar-Rahman ibn ‘Awf
A successful merchant who gave enormous wealth in Allah’s cause.
Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas
The first to shoot an arrow in Allah’s cause; commander at al-Qadisiyyah.
Sa‘id ibn Zayd
An early believer whose household helped bring ‘Umar to Islam.
Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah
Called the ‘trustee of this ummah’ by the Prophet ﷺ; commander in Syria.

trials.intro: He ﷺ said: “The most severely tested people are the Prophets, then the next best and the next best. A person is tested according to his religion” (Ibn Majah 4023, Tirmidhi 2398 — hasan sahih). Here is what the best of creation carried — so that no grief of ours is one he did not know.
stats: Of his 7 children died in his lifetime
Crescents seen with no fire lit in his homes
Of barley — his armour was pawned for food when he died

items.t: Born an orphan
items.s: His father ʿAbdullah died in Madinah before he was born. He never saw his father’s face.
items.you: Most people grow up with a father’s protection. He began life without it.
items.src: Ibn Hisham, as-Sirah; Ibn Saʿd, at-Tabaqat

items.t: His mother died before his eyes
items.s: Aminah took him to Madinah to visit his father’s grave. On the way back she fell ill and died at al-Abwaʾ. A six-year-old boy watched her buried in the desert. Decades later he visited her grave and wept, and those with him wept (Muslim 976).
items.you: Imagine losing your mother at six, far from home, on a journey.

items.t: His grandfather died
items.s: ʿAbd al-Muttalib, who took him in and loved him dearly, died two years later. The boy who had lost both parents now lost his guardian too.
items.you: Three deaths of the people raising him — before the age of nine.

items.t: His sons died as infants
items.s: Al-Qasim (by whom he was called Abu al-Qasim) and ʿAbdullah, his sons from Khadijah, died in early childhood in Makkah.
items.you: Burying a baby is the hardest grief a parent can know. He did it more than once.
items.src: Ibn Hisham; Ibn Saʿd; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah

items.t: The Year of Sorrow — uncle and wife in one year
items.s: Abu Talib, the uncle who raised and protected him for 40 years, died — refusing at the end to say lā ilāha illallāh while the Prophet ﷺ begged him to (Bukhari 3884). Within weeks his beloved wife Khadijah died — his first believer, comfort and support for 25 years. He never stopped speaking of her; he sent meat to her friends years after her death (Bukhari 3818).
items.you: Losing your protector and your life partner in the same season — while the whole city was against you.

items.t: His uncle Hamzah mutilated at Uhud
items.s: Hamzah — his uncle, foster-brother and “Lion of Allah” — was killed at Uhud by Wahshi’s spear, and his body was mutilated. Like other martyrs, he was buried with only a sheet too short to cover him (Bukhari 1274).
items.you: Seeing a loved one’s body desecrated is a pain few people ever face.

items.t: Three daughters buried
items.s: Ruqayyah died while he was at Badr. Zaynab died in 8 AH, and Umm Kulthum in 9 AH. He sat at Umm Kulthum’s grave with tears in his eyes (Bukhari 1285).
items.you: Of four daughters, he buried three. Only Fatimah outlived him — by six months.

items.t: His baby son Ibrahim died in his arms
items.s: Ibrahim, born to Mariyah, died at about 18 months. The Prophet ﷺ held him as he breathed his last; his eyes filled with tears. He said: “The eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord. O Ibrahim, we are saddened by your parting” (Bukhari 1303).
items.you: Six of his seven children died before him. He still taught us how to grieve with patience.

items.t: Camel entrails dumped on him in sujud
items.s: While he prostrated at the Kaʿbah, ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt threw the entrails of a slaughtered camel on his back. He stayed in sujud until his daughter Fatimah, still a girl, came and removed it while the Quraysh laughed (Bukhari 240, 3185).
items.you: Humiliated in the middle of prayer, in public, with his little daughter cleaning it off.

items.t: Strangled while praying
items.s: ʿUqbah twisted his cloth around the Prophet’s neck and strangled him hard until Abu Bakr pushed him off, saying: “Would you kill a man because he says: my Lord is Allah?” (Bukhari 3678).
items.you: Physically attacked for saying his Lord is Allah.

items.t: Three years of boycott in a valley
items.s: The Quraysh signed a pact: no trade, no marriage, no food with Banu Hashim. He and his family were confined to the valley of Abu Talib for about three years. They were so hungry that the companions later recalled eating leaves (Bukhari 3728).
items.you: Three years under siege with his wife and children, with hunger the daily reality.

items.t: Stoned at Taʾif — his hardest day
items.s: After the Year of Sorrow he walked to Taʾif to seek support. They mocked him and set children and slaves to stone him until his feet bled. Asked if he faced a day harder than Uhud, he named this day. When the angel of the mountains offered to crush the city, he refused: “I hope Allah will bring from their descendants people who worship Allah alone” (Bukhari 3231).
items.you: Bleeding, rejected, alone — and his response was mercy for their unborn children.

items.t: Assassination plots and the Hijrah
items.s: The Quraysh agreed on a plan for young men from every clan to kill him together. He left his home city by night, hid three days in the cave of Thawr with Abu Bakr, with a bounty of 100 camels on his head (Qur’an 8:30, 9:40; Bukhari 3905).
items.you: Forced out of the place he loved, hunted, with a price on his head.

items.t: Wounded at Uhud
items.s: His face was cut, his helmet broke into his head and a tooth was broken. Fatimah washed the blood and burned a mat to stop the bleeding (Bukhari 4075). Rumours spread that he had been killed.
items.you: Struck in battle, bleeding, while 70 companions lay dead around him.

items.t: Poisoned
items.s: A woman served him poisoned lamb. He forgave her for what she did to him, and said he felt the effect of that poison until his final illness (Bukhari 2617, 4428).
items.you: Someone tried to kill him over a meal — and the pain never fully left.

items.t: Magic worked on him
items.s: Labid ibn al-Aʿsam worked magic against him; for a period he felt affected, until Allah showed him its place and cure, and revealed the two protecting surahs (Bukhari 3268).
items.you: Even the unseen was used against him.

items.t: Called a liar, madman and sorcerer
items.s: His own people who had called him al-Amin (the trustworthy) now called him a poet, madman, sorcerer and liar. Allah comforted him: “We know that what they say grieves you” (Qur’an 6:33).
items.you: Character assassination by the people who once trusted him most.

items.t: His uncle Abu Lahab cursed him publicly
items.s: When he first called his clan to Islam on Mount Safa, his own uncle shouted: “May you perish! Is it for this you gathered us?” (Bukhari 4770). Abu Lahab followed him through markets telling people not to believe him.
items.you: Family turning on you, in public.

items.t: Watching his companions tortured
items.s: Bilal was dragged with a rock on his chest. Sumayyah — the first martyr — was killed; her husband Yasir died under torture; he could only say: “Patience, family of Yasir, your appointment is Paradise.”
items.you: Seeing the people you love suffer because they followed you.
items.src: Ibn Hisham; al-Hakim (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)

items.t: His wife slandered
items.s: Hypocrites spread a vile lie about ʿAʾishah. For a month revelation did not come, and he suffered in silence until Allah declared her innocence in Surah an-Nur (Bukhari 2637, 4750).
items.you: Gossip about your family spreading through the whole city.

items.t: Seventy companions murdered at Biʾr Maʿunah
items.s: About seventy Qur’an reciters he sent to teach were betrayed and killed. He was so grieved that he supplicated against the killers in prayer for a month (Bukhari 4088).
items.you: Losing seventy of your best students in one betrayal.

items.t: Months with no fire lit to cook
items.s: ʿAʾishah said: “We would see three crescent moons in two months and no fire was lit in the houses of the Messenger of Allah.” They lived on dates and water (Bukhari 2567, 6459).
items.you: Two months without a single cooked meal — as the leader of a nation.

items.t: A stone tied to his stomach
items.s: While digging the trench, he had a stone tied to his belly from hunger; they had not tasted food for three days (Bukhari 4101).
items.you: Working with his hands, starving, alongside his people.

items.t: Slept on a mat that marked his skin
items.s: ʿUmar found him lying on a palm-fibre mat that left marks on his side, with a leather pillow stuffed with fibre. ʿUmar wept, thinking of Persian and Roman kings. He said: “Are you not pleased that they have this world and we have the Hereafter?” (Bukhari 4913).
items.you: Ruler of Arabia, sleeping on a mat that left lines in his skin.

items.t: Died with his armour pawned for food
items.s: When he died, his iron armour was pawned to a Jewish man for thirty ṣāʿ of barley to feed his family (Bukhari 2916, 4467).
items.you: He gave away everything he received — and died in debt for barley.

items.t: Double the fever
items.s: Ibn Masʿud found him burning with fever: “I have as much fever as two of you.” “Is that because you have a double reward?” “Yes” (Bukhari 5648).
items.you: Even his sickness was harder than ours — and he still prayed for us.

deeds: “Shall I not be a grateful servant?” — when asked why, though Allah had forgiven him (Bukhari 4836).
He never hit a woman, a servant or anyone with his hand — except in battle for Allah (Muslim 2328).
“The best of you is the best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family” (Tirmidhi 3895, sahih).
Mercy to those who hurt him
At Taʾif he refused to destroy the people who stoned him (Bukhari 3231). He forgave the woman who poisoned him (Bukhari 2617).
Years after her death, he sent meat to her friends and spoke of her constantly (Bukhari 3818).
At the conquest of Makkah — the city that boycotted, tortured and expelled him — he declared a general pardon.
He prayed carrying Umamah, Zaynab’s daughter, setting her down in sujud (Muslim 543).
He died with nothing to inherit and his armour pawned for barley (Bukhari 2916).
forus: He raised his hands and wept: “O Allah, my Ummah, my Ummah.” Allah sent Jibril: “We will please you concerning your Ummah and not grieve you” (Muslim 202).
He saved his special du‘a for us
“Every prophet had a supplication that was answered, and I have kept mine as intercession for my Ummah on the Day of Resurrection” (Bukhari 6304, Muslim 199).

“I wish we could see our brothers.” They said: “Are we not your brothers?” He said: “You are my companions. My brothers are those who will come after me and believe in me without seeing me” (Muslim 249).
He made it easy for us
Fifty daily prayers became five on the night of Miʿraj because he kept returning to ask Allah to lighten it for us (Bukhari 3887).
He will intercede when no one else will
On the Day of Judgement every prophet will say “myself, myself” — he will say “my Ummah, my Ummah” and fall in sujud for us (Bukhari 4476, 7510).
trials.reflect: If you are grieving a parent, a child or a spouse; if you are mocked, poor, sick or betrayed — the Prophet ﷺ walked that road before you, and further. Send salawat upon him: “Whoever sends blessings upon me once, Allah sends blessings upon him ten times” (Muslim 408).
